# Introduction

Urban streams receive stormwater runoff that carries heavy metals, nutrients and fine sediment from roads and roofs (Walsh et al., 2005). In many cities, the installation of raingardens has been undertaken as a means of the reduction of these pollutant loads before they reach receiving waters. Although raingardens are widely promoted, and although several studies conducted in temperate climates under controlled laboratory conditions with synthetic stormwater have reported high removal efficiencies for total suspended solids, evidence from field installations in subtropical cities remains scarce.

It is important to note that raingarden performance may potentially depend on a number of possible factors. The filter media, the planting, the ratio of raingarden area to catchment area, and the age of the system all vary. Microbial communities in the filter media have also been proposed as drivers of nitrogen removal, but this has rarely been tested in the field.

Here we monitored twelve raingardens in Brisbane, Australia, over two wet seasons. Our aims were (1) to quantify the removal of total suspended solids, zinc and copper by field raingardens; (2) to test whether removal declines as raingardens age; and (3) to characterise the microbial communities of the filter media and relate them to nitrogen removal.

# Methods

The twelve raingardens, which were constructed between 2012 and 2020 by the city council as part of a water-sensitive urban design program and which range in area from 15 to 140 square metres, were sampled during storm events. Inflow and outflow samples were collected by ISCO autosamplers triggered by a flow threshold. TSS was determined gravimetrically following APHA method 2540D. Zinc and copper were measured by ICP-MS after acid digestion.

Each bioretention cell was assigned to an age class (young: under 4 years; mature: 4 to 8 years; old: over 8 years). Removal efficiency was calculated as the percentage reduction in event mean concentration between inflow and outflow. Differences between age classes were tested with a linear mixed model, with system as a random effect.

# Results

Across 84 storm events, the raingardens removed a median of 81% of TSS, 64% of zinc and 52% of copper. Removal of copper was more variable than removal of zinc, and in six events outflow copper concentrations exceeded inflow concentrations.

The young systems removed more zinc than the old systems (72% versus 55%; p = 0.03). TSS removal did not differ between age classes. The biofilters in the old class also had visibly more clogging of the surface layer.

# Discussion

Our results show that field raingardens in a subtropical city remove most of the sediment and much of the zinc in stormwater. This performance is comparable to laboratory studies, which suggests that laboratory results can be transferred to the field.

The decline in zinc removal with age indicates that raingardens become saturated with metals after about eight years, and that councils should therefore replace the filter media every eight years. Copper removal was lower and more variable, perhaps because copper binds to dissolved organic matter that passes through the filter media.

Raingardens could also provide habitat for urban pollinators, which would add to their value as green infrastructure. Future work should assess the cost-effectiveness of raingardens compared with conventional treatment.
